jsnvu6-e182545-d1e106.summary: Rubric for Question 2 of d.24: whether anything false can fall under faith, referring to Aquinas.

jsnvu6-e182545-d1e115.summary: Argument that falsehood can fall under faith: it can fall under hope, since one not in grace may hope for eternal life he will never have, and both are infused theological virtues.
claims: Hope can concern something false, so faith can too (objection)

jsnvu6-e182545-d1e133.summary: Second argument: future contingent truths can fail to occur, and many objects of faith, such as the judgment and the resurrection, are future contingents; so faith may concern something false.
claims: Future contingent articles of faith could fail to occur (objection)

jsnvu6-e182545-d1e147.summary: Argument for the opposite: the act of a virtue cannot be bad, but judging falsely is the evil of the intellect; so faith, an intellectual virtue, cannot assent to falsehood.
claims: A virtue's act cannot be false, since falsity is the intellect's evil

jsnvu6-e182545-d1e160.summary: Determination: nothing false can fall under the faith in question. (1) Faith and the vision of the blessed concern the same things in affirmation and negation, and nothing false falls under vision. (2) If faith concerns necessary truths, like the Trinity, they are immutable; if contingent ones, though they could fail by absolute power, they fall under faith only as related to divine ordination, under which they occur by necessity of supposition. (3) The middle of assent, the truth of divine authority, cannot fail, so the assent cannot be false.
claims: Nothing false can fall under theological faith
Faith and beatific vision concern the same objects
Contingent articles fall under faith only as subject to divine ordination, under which they are necessary by supposition
Divine authority, the middle of faith, cannot fail

jsnvu6-e182545-d1e215.summary: Replies: (1) Falsity cannot fall under hope either, but for a different reason: truth and falsity belong to the intellect, not the will, so an act of hope is not false even if the hoped-for does not come, though it may follow a false estimate, as with hoping for a good dinner. Alternatively, infused hope hopes for eternal life through Christ's grace persevering, which never fails; the first answer is perhaps better. (2) Future contingents fall under faith only as subject to divine ordination, and so cannot fail. Whether faith can concern things known scientifically was treated in Book 1, q.1; whether it can concern things seen will be treated in d.31.
claims: Truth and falsity belong to acts of intellect, not of will
Hope is not false even if its object fails; at most the accompanying estimate is
Infused hope is for eternal life through persevering grace
Future contingents fall under faith only as divinely ordained
concepts: truth and falsity in intellect vs. will

jsnvu6-e182545.summary: Question 2 of d.24 asks whether anything false can fall under faith. Durandus answers that nothing false can fall under theological faith, for three reasons. Faith and beatific vision concern the same things affirmatively and negatively. Necessary articles are immutable, and contingent ones fall under faith only as they relate to divine ordination, under which they are necessary by supposition. Faith's middle, the truth of divine authority, cannot fail. Against the analogy with hope, he argues that truth and falsity belong to the intellect, not the will: hope is never properly false, though it may follow a false estimate, and infused hope concerns salvation through persevering grace. Future contingent articles, such as the resurrection and judgment, cannot fail as divinely ordained.
claims: Nothing false can fall under theological faith
Contingent articles of faith are necessary by supposition of divine ordination
Divine authority, the middle of faith, cannot fail
Truth and falsity belong properly to the intellect, not the will
